paper_metadata.title: A Holy Quran Ontology Construction with Semi-Automatic Population

evidence.excerpt: DOI information is associated with the journal article as 10.21786/bbrc/12.1/26.

paper_metadata.abstract: The paper proposes a semi-automatic method for constructing and populating an ontology of named entities in the Holy Quran. It combines learning methods with statistical context ranking to discover additional named entities from the Quran and Hadith, followed by expert validation.

problem_addressed: Manual ontology population is time-consuming, while existing Quran ontologies do not contain all named-entity instances. The paper addresses construction of a named-entity ontology for the Holy Quran and semi-automatic discovery and population of additional instances using Quranic text and Sahih Al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim Hadith collections.

methodology.description: The authors first define the ontology domain and scope, reuse selected concepts from the Quran Corpus ontology, identify terms, build a hierarchical class taxonomy, define attributes and values, and then populate the ontology. Initial confident instances seed an iterative semi-automatic process. The system finds their occurrences in the Quran and two Hadith collections, extracts surrounding n-word contexts, ranks contexts using a TF-IDF-derived frequency scheme, searches for text segments matching retained contexts, treats matches as candidate named-entity instances, and sends candidates to an Islamic-knowledge expert for validation. Validated instances are added to the seed set and the process repeats. The ontology is implemented in Protégé 2000 and includes classes, subclasses, individuals, binary object properties, and class-equivalence constructs. The figures show the UML/class structure, class hierarchy, individuals, object properties, OWL equivalent-class representation, and OntoGraf visualizations.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: The target schema is NEQ-Ontology, an ontology of named entities in the Holy Quran and Hadith. The authors reuse some concepts from the Quran Corpus ontology but create a new taxonomy and populate missing instances. The ontology defines 15 superclasses, hierarchical subclasses, class attributes, attribute values, binary object properties, and equivalent-class descriptions represented in OWL. Examples include Person/Prophet, Animal/Cow, Book, color properties, and relations such as SenderTo and has Miraculous.

text_to_kg_stages: Ontology or schema discovery: define the named-entity domain, terms, class hierarchy, attributes, values, and relations.
Text preprocessing: search the Quran and Hadith collections for occurrences of seed instances.
Entity and concept extraction: identify context-matching segments as candidate named entities.
Entity typing: assign validated instances to ontology classes or subclasses.
Relation and triple extraction: define and populate binary object properties between individuals; the paper illustrates relations such as has Color, SenderTo, and has Miraculous.
Graph construction: represent classes, subclasses, individuals, attributes, and object properties in NEQ-Ontology/OWL.
Graph validation and correction: expert in Islamic knowledge validates candidate instances.
Graph updating: add validated instances to the seed set and iterate context learning and extraction.

input_output.input_type: Unstructured natural-language religious texts: the Holy Quran, Sahih Al-Bukhari, and Sahih Muslim Hadith collections.
input_output.input_granularity: Document collections and text occurrences of known named entities; contexts are fixed-width windows of n words preceding and following each entity occurrence, and matching text segments are used for candidate discovery.
input_output.output_representation: A populated NEQ-Ontology represented as an ontology/OWL knowledge structure containing 15 superclasses, hierarchical subclasses, individuals, class attributes and values, binary object properties, and equivalent-class descriptions.

models_and_tools: Learning techniques for acquiring and classifying ontology instances
Statistical context ranking based on TF-IDF-related context frequency, inverse context frequency, example frequency, and inverse example frequency

evaluation.setting: The paper reports an implementation and illustrative ontology examples, including class hierarchies, individuals, object properties, equivalent-class modeling, and OntoGraf visualizations. It does not describe a quantitative named-entity extraction evaluation, a held-out test set, train/test split, or comparison against baselines.

value: The authors construct NEQ-Ontology for named entities in the Holy Quran and Hadith.
The ontology reuses selected Quran Corpus concepts while adding a new taxonomy and additional named-entity instances from Quran and Hadith sources.
The proposed iterative method uses seed instances, context extraction, TF-IDF-based context ranking, context matching, and expert validation to extend the instance set.
The implementation models 15 superclasses with subclasses, individuals, attributes, binary object properties, and equivalent-class descriptions, and provides Protégé/OntoGraf visualizations.
No numerical precision, recall, F1, coverage, or comparative performance results are reported.

value: Uses authoritative domain texts from the Quran and two Hadith collections to extend a Quranic named-entity ontology.
Reduces fully manual population by iteratively exploiting contexts around trusted seed instances.
Includes domain-expert validation before candidate instances are incorporated.
Provides an explicit ontology construction workflow and a concrete graph representation with classes, instances, properties, and OWL equivalence.
The approach is domain-oriented and supports subsequent Quran information retrieval, information extraction, and text-mining applications.

value: The method is limited to discovering additional named-entity instances from context patterns; it does not automatically discover new ontology classes.
The paper does not provide quantitative extraction or ontology-population evaluation, benchmark splits, error analysis, or baseline comparison.
The process depends on a small manually selected seed set and expert validation, limiting full automation and potentially affecting scalability.
Context matching and TF-IDF ranking may identify candidates based on surface context without demonstrating semantic disambiguation or robust relation extraction.
The paper does not establish exhaustive coverage of named entities in the Quran.
